newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl's govt, opposition to keep talking on taxes.
newsitem.headline: Kohl's govt, opposition to keep talking on taxes.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition and Germany's main opposition parties on Thursday agreed to meet later this month in parliament's mediation committee to try to hammer out a compromise on the government's tax reform.

Struggling to get the economy in shape for European economic and monetary union, Finance Minister Theo Waigel hopes to kick-start investment with income tax cuts and offset some of the lost revenue by plugging loopholes and tax write-offs.

Government legislation to cut income taxes by some 30 billion marks over the next two years passed in the lower house, or Bundestag, last month, but was then blocked by the opposition-controlled upper house, or Bundesrat.
Waigel, speaking on the sidelines of a meeting of the mediation committee of both houses of parliament, would not comment on the talks but said the two sides would meet again.
"The working groups will be set up and then we will see how things are at the end of July," he said.
The committee, made up of 32 members divided equally between both houses of parliament, meets next on July 30.

The Social Democrats (SPD), the main opposition in the lower house, control the Bundesrat because they rule a majority of federal states. Counting deputies from the environmentalist Greens, the opposition parties have a majority in the mediation committee and could therefore block passage of the legislation.

The German Federation of Chambers of Commerce (DIHT), Federation of German Industry (BDI), Federation of Employers' Associations (BDA) and the Federation of Skilled Craftsmen and Tradesmen (ZDH) warned both sides their decision was crucial to improving German industry's ability to compete internationally.

"From industry's point of view if the tax reform fails in parliamentary mediation it will have drastic consequences for companies' willingness to invest in Germany and will scare off foreign investors even more," they said in a joint statement.
But prospects looked dim for a compromise between Kohl's coalition and the opposition after pre-mediation talks on Tuesday broke down, mediation committee chairman Heribert Blens said.
Blens told German Radio mediation could last for weeks and that, if it were to reach a compromise, the lower house could call a special session in August to vote on it.

Should the lower house reject a compromise, the bills cannot become law, but it would still be possible to reopen the mediation procedure, although this is considered unlikely before the general elections in 1998.
With prospects for a broad agreement waning, opposition and coalition parties have begun talking of reaching agreement where possible, so as not to scuttle the whole project.

"The abolition of trading capital tax for companies is one bill which we on the mediation committee have discussed for a long time. I am optimistic that we will reach a good result on this," Blens said.
Blens said there was also a chance of making progress on reducing supplementary wage costs -- one factor that makes wages in western Germany among the highest internationally.
Kohl's junior coalition partners the Free Democrats (FDP), Germany's self-styled party of tax-cutting, have ruled out a reform involving tax hikes to finance other reductions.
FDP parliamentary leader Hermann-Otto Solms told Berlin's InfoRadio his party, on which Kohl relies for his 12-seat majority, was not going to change its tough position on this.
"It is unacceptable to come up with a re-distribution which means taxpayers, who already pay too much, should come out of this empty-handed," Solms said in an interview.
"All the experts say we need a reduction in taxes and social and health contributions to create a better investment climate, jobs can only be created through investment," he said.
-- Bonn Newsroom, 49 228 26097 150
